title: Om

teacherSummary.text: Still aching for his son, Siddhartha sees his reflection resemble his own father and understands the circle of suffering. He confesses everything to Vasudeva, who leads him to listen; the river's voices—joy and sorrow, good and evil—blend into one word, Om. Siddhartha achieves serenity. Vasudeva, his work done, goes “into the forests,” “into the oneness” (Om, paragraph 24).

items.lookFor: Sitting and weaving a basket
followUps: Where exactly does it say that? Read us the line.
Who can add a detail that comes just before or after?
items.answerGuidance: “Vasudeva was sitting in the hut and weaving a basket.” (Om, paragraph 8)

items.text: Whose images does Siddhartha see merge in the river as he listens better?
items.lookFor: His father’s, his own and his son’s; then Kamala’s and Govinda’s
followUps: Where exactly does it say that? Read us the line.
Who can add a detail that comes just before or after?
items.answerGuidance: “The image of his father, his own image, the image of his son merged, Kamala’s image also appeared” (Om, paragraph 16).

items.text: What does Siddhartha feel flowing over to Vasudeva as he speaks?
items.lookFor: His pain and his fears
followUps: Where exactly does it say that? Read us the line.
Who can add a detail that comes just before or after?
items.answerGuidance: His pain and fear: “he sensed how his pain, his fears flowed over to him, how his secret hope flowed over” (Om, paragraph 10).

items.text: What does Vasudeva see shining in Siddhartha’s eyes when he rises from the seat by the bank?
items.lookFor: The cheerfulness of the knowledge
followUps: Where exactly does it say that? Read us the line.
Who can add a detail that comes just before or after?
items.answerGuidance: He “saw the cheerfulness of the knowledge shining in them” (Om, paragraph 21).

items.text: Retell the three most important events of “Om” in order, in one sentence each.
items.lookFor: Still aching for his son, Siddhartha sees his reflection resemble his own father and understands the circle of suffering. He confesses everything to Vasudeva, who leads him to listen; the river's voices—joy and sorrow, good and evil—blend into one word, Om. Siddhartha achieves serenity. Vasudeva, his work done, goes “into the forests,” “into the oneness” (Om, paragraph 24).
followUps: Where exactly does it say that? Read us the line.
Who can add a detail that comes just before or after?
items.answerGuidance: Siddhartha still aches for his son and sets off for the city, but the river laughs and he turns back (Om, paragraphs 4–6); he tells Vasudeva everything (paragraphs 7–10); listening together, he hears all voices become Om, and Vasudeva leaves for the forest (paragraphs 13–25).

items.text: Which characters appear or are mentioned in “Om”? Name two and one thing each says or does.
items.lookFor: Names and actions taken from the chapter; check against the teacher summary.
followUps: Where exactly does it say that? Read us the line.
Who can add a detail that comes just before or after?
items.answerGuidance: Two of: Vasudeva, who listens and then says farewell (paragraphs 10, 21–24); the son, whose image he sees in the river (paragraph 13); his father, whose face he sees in his own reflection (paragraph 5).

items.text: Where and when does “Om” take place? Point to the line that tells you.
items.lookFor: A place/time detail quoted from the chapter.
followUps: Where exactly does it say that? Read us the line.
Who can add a detail that comes just before or after?
items.answerGuidance: At the river and Vasudeva’s hut, in the dry season, years after the son leaves: “it was the dry season, but its voice sounded strange: it laughed!” (Om, paragraph 5)

items.text: Reread: “Slowly this blossomed in him, was shining back at him from Vasudeva’s old, childlike face: harmony, knowledge of the eternal perfection of the world, smiling, oneness.” What does “harmony” mean here, and what is literally happening in this line?
items.lookFor: harmony: a peaceful agreement of all the parts.
followUps: Where exactly does it say that? Read us the line.
Who can add a detail that comes just before or after?
items.answerGuidance: “Harmony” here means: a peaceful agreement of all the parts. In Om, paragraph 3, Siddhartha sees in Vasudeva’s face the calm unity he is beginning to understand.

items.text: Reread: “Was it not a comedy, a strange and stupid matter, this repetition, this running around in a fateful circle?” What does “repetition” mean here, and what is literally happening in this line?
items.lookFor: repetition: doing or living the same thing again.
followUps: Where exactly does it say that? Read us the line.
Who can add a detail that comes just before or after?
items.answerGuidance: “Repetition” here means: doing or living the same thing again. In Om, paragraph 5, he sees that he is now suffering over his son just as his father once suffered over him, the same pattern again.

items.text: What does “Om” suggest about hearing the many voices? State the inference and the line that supports it.
items.lookFor: A stated inference (for example, that hearing all voices together is the end of the search) backed by one located line, such as the one in Om, paragraph 17.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: The chapter suggests that hearing all voices together is the end of the search. Support: “everything was one, everything was intertwined and connected, entangled a thousand times” (Om, paragraph 17).

items.text: Find one example of symbolism in this chapter. What does it reveal that a plain statement would not?
items.lookFor: Look for objects, places or actions that stand for larger ideas.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: The river’s laughter (“The river laughed.” (Om, paragraph 6)) stands for the mockery of his repeating pain; a statement would not carry how the same pain returns ‘over and over again.’

items.text: How does the imagery in this chapter shape what we understand about hearing the many voices?
items.lookFor: Look for sensory details (sight, sound, cold, light) and what mood they create.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: Images of faces merging in the water (“The image of his father, his own image, the image of his son merged” (Om, paragraph 16)) make the unity of all lives visible.

items.text: In the passage that begins “Slowly blossomed, slowly ripened in Siddhartha the realisation, the knowledge, what wisdom actually was, what the goal of his long search was.”, why might Hesse have chosen these particular words? Pick two and explain their connotations.
items.lookFor: Diction analysis of two words in the anchor passage.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: In Om, paragraph 3, the doubled “slowly blossomed, slowly ripened” makes wisdom grow like a plant, not arrive as a lesson.

items.text: What causes the main turn in “Om”, and what effect is it likely to have on what follows?
items.lookFor: Still aching for his son, Siddhartha sees his reflection resemble his own father and understands the circle of suffering. He confesses everything to Vasudeva, who leads him to listen; the river's voices—joy and sorrow, good and evil—blend into one word, Om. Siddhartha achieves serenity. Vasudeva,…
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: The cause is his confession and the listening at the river (Om, paragraphs 9–17). Effect: he stops fighting his fate (paragraph 20), and Vasudeva can leave him in charge of the ferry.

items.text: How does “Om” build on “The Son”? Name one link of cause and effect.
items.lookFor: A causal or structural link between this and the previous chapter.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: Cause and effect: the wound from “The Son” still burns (“For a long time, the wound continued to burn.” (Om, paragraph 1)) and drives him toward the city, where the river turns him back.

items.text: What can we infer about a character's motives from what they say and do here, as opposed to what they claim?
items.lookFor: An inference about motive supported by a quoted line.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: Siddhartha claims he only wants to see his son, but his envy of fathers (paragraph 1) shows longing for his own happiness; Vasudeva says little, but his waiting for “this hour” (paragraph 21) shows his purpose was to help Siddhartha reach it.

items.text: The bell-ringer asked: “What does Siddhartha finally understand when he hears all the voices together?” Now that we have read closely, how would you revise your first answer, and which line changed your mind?
items.lookFor: A revised answer anchored in the text.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: A revised answer should go beyond ‘everything is one’ to what that means for him: pain, joy and longing belong together, so he stops resisting his fate (Om, paragraphs 17 and 20).

items.text: Where does theme appear, and how does it connect this chapter to the larger concern with the search for self-knowledge?
items.lookFor: Look for statements or moments that connect to the book's big ideas.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: The theme of oneness appears in the merging voices (Om, paragraph 17) and in the definition of wisdom in paragraph 3: “to think every moment, while living his life, the thought of oneness” (Om, paragraph 3).

items.text: Background: Hesse blends Hindu and Buddhist ideas of unity with Western mysticism. How does knowing this change the way you read one moment in the chapter?
items.lookFor: A specific moment reread in light of the context.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: Knowing Hesse blends traditions explains why Om, a Hindu syllable, crowns a Buddhist-style insight (paragraph 19): the chapter presents unity as larger than any one teaching.

items.text: A critic might argue: “The climax: all opposites unite into one harmony, and the student becomes the master.” How far do you agree? Take a stand and defend it with two lines from the chapter.
items.lookFor: A defended position with evidence and one counterpoint.
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?
items.answerGuidance: Agree: the voices unite into Om (paragraphs 17–19). A text counterpoint: the chapter begins with a wound that ‘would not go out by itself’ (paragraph 4), so the harmony is earned through pain, not simply given.

items.text: Which character in this chapter acts most wisely, and which least? Judge them by a standard you name.
items.lookFor: An evaluation using an explicit criterion and evidence.
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?
items.answerGuidance: With listening as the standard, Vasudeva is wisest (paragraphs 10–15); Siddhartha least when he sets off to chase his son (paragraph 5), though he turns back himself.

items.text: Rewrite one moment of “Om” from the point of view of a different character. What does the new angle reveal or hide about hearing the many voices?
items.lookFor: A rewrite that keeps the chapter’s events accurate, speaks in the chosen character’s voice, and ends with a sentence on what the new angle shows or hides.
followUps: Which line from the chapter does your piece depend on? Read it to us.
What did you keep from the original, and what did you change on purpose?
items.answerGuidance: Vasudeva’s view of the listening (Om, paragraphs 11–21) works well: it shows patience and joy and hides the struggle inside Siddhartha.

items.text: Write three questions of your own about “Om”: one recall, one “why/how”, and one “should/what if”. Trade with a partner and answer theirs.
items.lookFor: Three questions at three levels, each answerable from the chapter, traded and answered with a line.
followUps: Which of your three questions was hardest to answer from the text, and why?
Which line did your partner use, and does it really answer your why/how question?
items.answerGuidance: Example set: recall, ‘What does Vasudeva do at the end?’ (goes into the forest, paragraph 24); why/how, ‘Why does the river laugh?’ (paragraph 6); what if, ‘Should Siddhartha have gone to the city?’

items.text: Connect this chapter to experience versus teaching: is the link strong or weak so far? What would Hesse need to show next to strengthen it?
items.lookFor: A judgment of thematic development across the work.
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?
items.answerGuidance: Strong: no one teaches him; Vasudeva only says “Listen better!” (paragraph 15) and the experience does the rest.

items.text: Is the symbolism in this chapter effective, or does it feel heavy-handed? Evaluate it as a reader would in a review.
items.lookFor: An evaluative judgment with criteria and evidence.
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?
items.answerGuidance: Effective for many readers: the laughing river and merging faces are concrete. Some find the Om finale (paragraph 19) abstract.

items.text: Compare how “Om” treats hearing the many voices with how another text, film or event you know treats a similar idea. What does Siddhartha see that the other misses?
items.lookFor: A cross-text synthesis.
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?
items.answerGuidance: A comparison should name a moment when a character hears or sees everything at once and quote “everything was one” (Om, paragraph 17); Siddhartha’s version ends in calm acceptance, not ecstasy.

items.text: Predict what “Govinda” will bring, using two clues from this chapter. After reading, evaluate your prediction.
items.lookFor: A prediction or judgment justified with textual clues.
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?
items.answerGuidance: Clues: Vasudeva leaves and Siddhartha remains as the ferryman (paragraphs 24–25), and he now looks on others with sympathy (paragraph 2). Prediction: someone from his past will come to the river and see his change.

items.text: Design a one-paragraph modern adaptation of this chapter (setting, characters, conflict). What must stay the same for it to still be about hearing the many voices?
items.lookFor: A modern setting, characters and conflict that keep the chapter’s core idea, with the one element that must not change named.
followUps: Which line from the chapter does your piece depend on? Read it to us.
What did you keep from the original, and what did you change on purpose?
items.answerGuidance: A modern version keeps a grieving parent who finally lets go after listening with an old friend. What must stay is the moment of stopping the fight with fate (paragraph 20).

items.text: What question would you most like to ask Hermann Hesse about this chapter, and what answer do you think the text itself gives?
items.lookFor: A student-generated question answered from evidence.
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?
items.answerGuidance: Example: ‘What did Siddhartha actually learn from the river?’ The text answers in paragraph 3: wisdom is the readiness to feel oneness in every moment.

hsSophomore.note: Require a quotation and an explanation; push evaluative answers to address a counterclaim.

hsJunior.note: Emphasize structure and ambiguity; students should name where the text leaves matters open.

hsSenior.note: Weigh competing interpretations; students should defend the stronger reading.

ap.note: Treat each evaluative item as a thesis rehearsal: defensible claim, purposeful evidence, commentary on choices.

collegeFreshman.note: Add the extension: connect answers to historical context and one secondary perspective.

collegeSophomore.note: Use the extensions: genre and period conventions, and a published critic.

collegeJunior.note: Use the extensions: name a critical method and test it against the passage.

collegeSenior.note: Use the extensions: connect the chapter to the whole work and the scholarship.

graduate.note: Use the extensions: position answers in a critical conversation and the textual history.

rows.objective: Analyze how seeing his father's face in his reflection changes him. *(theme)*
Analyze how the many voices become one word, Om. *(struct)*
Argue how Vasudeva's departure completes the teaching.
Write a paragraph on unity in Om.

Explain the repetition of father and son and the river’s many voices becoming Om, using “All of it together was the flow of events, was the music of life.” (Hesse, 1922/2015, Om, para. 17), and compare one critical voice from this unit.

Apply a formal reading to the repetition of father and son and the river’s many voices becoming Om: show how imagery and repetition in “All of it together was the flow of events, was the music of life.” (Hesse, 1922/2015, Om, para. 17) build its meaning.

Argue how the repetition of father and son and the river’s many voices becoming Om advances the novel’s claim about teaching versus experience, testing “All of it together was the flow of events, was the music of life.” (Hesse, 1922/2015, Om, para. 17) against one later chapter.

Situate the repetition of father and son and the river’s many voices becoming Om within scholarship on Hesse and European representations of Indian thought, stating method and contribution, with “All of it together was the flow of events, was the music of life.” (Hesse, 1922/2015, Om, para. 17) as anchor.
